adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:37 — Concurrent feed imports can interleave post revisions and digest writes, leaving content mismatched with its saved digest and causing subsequent polls to skip the needed correction.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the import method in topic_embed.rb, when updating an existing embed (lines 31-37), the code calls revisor.revise! and then embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1). These are two separate database operations not wrapped in a transaction. If two concurrent processes are importing the same URL with different content, they could interleave: Process A revises post, Process B revises post, Process A updates digest, Process B updates digest. This leaves the content_sha1 potentially mismatched with the actual post content. The creation path uses Topic.transaction but the update path does not have similar protection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:148 — Replacing the importer removes its `--category`/`-c` option and stops assigning the selected category, so existing scripted imports now fail or silently land in the default category.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows that in lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the `method_option :category` line is removed (line 117 in the old file), and the code that used `options[:category]` to set `category_id` (lines 144-147) is also removed. The import method now uses `TopicEmbed.import_remote` instead of `PostCreator.new` with a category parameter. This means existing scripts using `--category` or `-c` flags will fail (unrecognized option) or the category assignment will be silently ignored, breaking backward compatibility.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:65 — URL conversion rewrites scheme-relative links and images such as //cdn.example.com/image.png onto the article host, breaking imported content.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in topic_embed.rb lines 56-72, the absolutize_urls method checks `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')` and `if src.present? && src.start_with?('/')`. A scheme-relative URL like `//cdn.example.com/image.png` starts with '/' so it would match this condition and get incorrectly rewritten to `http://eviltrout.com/cdn.example.com/image.png` (after stripping leading slashes). This is a real bug - scheme-relative URLs should be preserved or handled differently, not treated as relative paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:64 — Document-relative links and image sources are left unchanged and therefore resolve against the forum instead of the source article.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 53-71, the code only converts URLs that start with '/' (absolute paths). The condition `if href.present? && href.start_with?('/')` means document-relative links (like 'hello' without a leading slash, or '../page') are not converted. The test in the spec shows contents with '/hello' and '/images/wat.jpg' which both start with '/' and get converted correctly. However, if the source article had truly relative URLs like 'hello' or 'images/wat.jpg' (without leading slash), they would not be converted and would resolve incorrectly against the forum's domain. This is a real bug in the URL absolutization logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:3 — force: true` drops any pre-existing `topic_embeds` table before recreating it, destroying imported-topic records during migration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `force: true` in the migration will destroy existing topic_embeds records. However, this is a new migration creating a new table for a new feature. At the time this migration runs, there would be no pre-existing topic_embeds table with data to destroy - this is the initial creation of the table. The `force: true` option is commonly used in migrations to ensure clean table creation and is not a bug in this context since no data would exist yet.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 — Adding `force: true` makes this migration drop and recreate an existing `top_topics` table, erasing its cached topic data instead of failing safely.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `create_table :top_topics, force: true` being added in db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb. The `force: true` option in Rails migrations causes the table to be dropped if it already exists before creating it. This is dangerous in a production migration because if the migration is run again (e.g., during a rollback/re-run scenario) or if the table already exists, it will destroy all existing data in the top_topics table. This is a real defect that could cause data loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — TopicRetriever synchronously invokes the scheduled PollFeed job, coupling single-page retrieval to full-feed import policy and making future job lifecycle changes affect embeds.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 38-41, the perform_retrieve method synchronously calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) directly rather than enqueueing it. This is a valid architectural concern - the TopicRetriever (used for single embed URL retrieval) directly invokes the full feed polling job synchronously, which creates coupling between these two different use cases. This could cause issues if the PollFeed job's behavior changes, and it means a single embed request could trigger processing of an entire RSS feed. However, this appears to be intentional design (checking if the URL exists in the feed first before doing HTTP fetch), so it's a design/architecture concern rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:20 — feed_key is newly added but never read, leaving dead cache-key code that obscures whether feed polling has an intended incremental-fetch contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims feed_key is 'never read' and is 'dead code'. Looking at the diff, feed_key is defined as a method in poll_feed.rb (lines 20-22) that generates a cache key. While it's true that feed_key is not used within the visible diff, this doesn't mean it's dead code - it could be intended for future use or the implementation may be incomplete. However, the finding overstates this as a definite problem. The method is simply defined but not yet utilized in this initial implementation. This is more of a minor observation about potentially unused code rather than a verifiable bug or important issue. The claim about 'obscuring incremental-fetch contract' is speculative and not grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:62 — URL normalization duplicates the same root-relative rewrite loop for anchors and images, so later URL-rule changes can drift between the two content types.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 56-68, there are two nearly identical loops - one for 'a' tags (href attribute) and one for 'img' tags (src attribute). Both loops perform the same URL normalization logic (checking if the attribute starts with '/' and prepending the prefix). This is code duplication that could lead to drift if one is updated but not the other. However, this is a maintainability/code quality concern rather than a bug - the current code works correctly. It's a valid architectural observation about the new code in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:41 — Each cache-miss retrieval runs the entire feed poll before checking the requested URL, so concurrent new embeds multiply full-feed parsing and per-item import work and can saturate job workers.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 38-41, perform_retrieve calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}) which processes the entire RSS feed (parsing all items and calling TopicEmbed.import for each) before checking if the specific embed_url exists. This is inefficient - if multiple concurrent requests come in for different new URLs, each will trigger a full feed poll. However, this is an architectural/performance concern rather than a bug - the code functions correctly, just inefficiently. The throttling mechanism (retrieved_recently?) only prevents repeated requests for the same URL, not concurrent requests for different URLs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — Reading a remote page without a response-size limit materializes arbitrary configured-host content before Readability parses it, allowing a large page to exhaust a worker's memory.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48, the code uses `open(url).read` to fetch remote content without any size limit. This is visible in the diff: `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. A malicious or misconfigured embeddable host could serve an extremely large page that would be fully read into memory before Readability processes it, potentially exhausting worker memory. This is a real security/resource exhaustion vulnerability in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — The remote page fetch has no open or read timeout, so an unresponsive source can hold a retrieval worker indefinitely and exhaust the background queue.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48: `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. The `open(url)` call uses Ruby's open-uri without any timeout options specified. This means if the remote server is slow or unresponsive, the worker thread will block indefinitely. This is a real defect that could exhaust background job workers when fetching from unresponsive URLs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:29 — The feed fetch has no open or read timeout, so a stalled feed server can indefinitely block the scheduled poll and imports.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 29, the code uses `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` from the 'open-uri' library without specifying any timeout options. The open-uri library's `open` method can indeed block indefinitely if the remote server is slow or unresponsive. This is a real defect - a stalled feed server could block the scheduled job worker indefinitely, preventing other scheduled jobs from running and potentially causing resource exhaustion. The fix would be to add timeout options like `open(url, read_timeout: 30, open_timeout: 10)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:27 — A process failure between SETNX and EXPIRE leaves the retrieval throttle key without a TTL, permanently suppressing future imports for that URL.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in lib/topic_retriever.rb lines 25-30 that SETNX and EXPIRE are called as separate operations. If the process crashes or fails between these two calls, the key will be set without a TTL, causing it to persist indefinitely. This would permanently block retrieval for that specific embed_url. This is a real race condition bug - Redis provides SET with NX and EX options together to avoid this exact issue, but the code uses the two-step approach.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/views/embed/loading.html.erb:9 — Failed retrievals have no terminal state, so this unconditional reload repeatedly enqueues work and leaves embeds loading until the source recovers.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in app/views/embed/loading.html.erb, there's an unconditional setTimeout that reloads the page every 30 seconds. Looking at the embed_controller.rb, when TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed returns nil, it enqueues a RetrieveTopic job and renders 'loading'. If the retrieval fails (e.g., invalid URL, network error, or the source site is down), the topic_id will remain nil, and each reload will re-enqueue the job and show loading again indefinitely. There's no mechanism to detect or handle permanent failures, leading to infinite reload loops and repeated job enqueueing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:22 — Feed HTML is saved with raw_html cooking without sanitization, so scripts or event handlers supplied by a feed author execute in the forum origin.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 22 that PostCreator is called with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Looking at app/models/post.rb lines 131-133, when cook_method is raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any processing. The content comes from RSS feeds (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb) or remote URLs (import_remote method) and is stored as raw HTML. There's no sanitization visible in the diff - the content goes through CGI.unescapeHTML and absolutize_urls but no HTML sanitization. This means malicious scripts or event handlers in feed content would execute in the forum's origin, which is a real XSS security vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:48 — open(url) follows redirects without revalidating the destination, allowing an allowed-host redirect to fetch internal services and publish their contents as a topic.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 48: `doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. The `open(url)` call using Kernel#open (or open-uri) will follow HTTP redirects automatically. If an attacker controls a URL on the allowed embeddable_host, they could redirect to internal services (e.g., http://localhost:9200, internal metadata endpoints, etc.). The content from those internal services would then be imported and published as a topic, constituting a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. The code only validates the initial URL's host against embeddable_host but doesn't validate redirect destinations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:41 — The test expects a direct `TopicRetriever` call even though `best` only enqueues `:retrieve_topic`, so it fails or misses the queued URL/user payload.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:41, it expects TopicRetriever.new to be called and retriever.retrieve to be invoked. Looking at the controller code in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb, when topic_id is nil, it calls Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) which enqueues a job. The test mocks TopicRetriever directly, but the controller actually enqueues a job. However, examining the test more carefully, the test stubs TopicEmbed.expects(:topic_id_for_embed).returns(nil) and then expects TopicRetriever to be called directly. The controller code shows Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...) is called instead. But the test passes because it's mocking the expectations - it expects TopicRetriever.new.returns(retriever) and retriever.expects(:retrieve). This is actually testing the wrong thing (the job, not the controller), but the finding claims the test 'fails or misses the queued URL/user payload' which is not accurate - the test would actually fail because TopicRetriever is never directly instantiated by the controller. However, looking at the test setup with mocks, the test would pass because it's using expects() which sets up expectations. The finding is partially correct that there's a mismatch, but the characterization is imprecise. The test does mock TopicRetriever but the controller enqueues a job instead - this is a test design issue but the finding's specific claim about 'fails or misses the queued URL/user payload' is not quite right.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb:9 — No spec exercises the new queued retrieval job, leaving its required URL validation and staff throttle bypass able to regress without detection.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new job class `RetrieveTopic` in `app/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb` with specific logic including URL validation (`raise Discourse::InvalidParameters.new(:embed_url) unless args[:embed_url].present?`) and staff throttle bypass (`no_throttle: user.try(:staff?)`). Looking at the test files added in the diff, there is `spec/components/topic_retriever_spec.rb` which tests `TopicRetriever`, and `spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb` which tests `PollFeed`, but there is no `spec/jobs/retrieve_topic_spec.rb` or similar test file for the `RetrieveTopic` job. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb:31 — The poller specs mock `poll_feed`, so feed parsing and item import behavior, including the `link`-to-`id` fallback, can regress while the tests pass.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that spec/jobs/poll_feed_spec.rb only tests that poll_feed is called under certain conditions by mocking it with `poller.expects(:poll_feed)`. Looking at the actual poll_feed implementation in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb (lines 23-37), there's real logic including RSS parsing, the link-to-id fallback (`url = i.id if url.blank? || url !~ /^https?\:\/\//`), and content processing. The test file shown in the diff doesn't test any of this actual parsing behavior - it only verifies the execute method delegates to poll_feed. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/topic_retriever_spec.rb:32 — The retriever specs mock `perform_retrieve`, leaving the new existing-embed, feed lookup, and remote-fetch branches unverified when embedded discussions need loading.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test at spec/components/topic_retriever_spec.rb mocks `perform_retrieve` (lines 32 and 39), which means the actual implementation of `perform_retrieve` in lib/topic_retriever.rb (lines 33-47) is never tested. This implementation contains important logic: checking if TopicEmbed already exists, optionally polling RSS feed, and calling fetch_http. These are new code paths introduced in this diff that lack test coverage. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added nontrivial logic.
